text:
On February 12th, 1966, I stood in the women's section of Temple Beth Sholom in Southfield, eight months pregnant, waiting for Rabbi Adler to finish a sentence he had been finishing for twenty years.

The sanctuary that morning smelled of wood polish and wool coats, the way it smelled every Saturday, with the addition of February, which is to say the smell of cold things being carried indoors. There were maybe ninety people in the room. Mrs. Abramson stood beside me, her hat tilted back the way she wore it so people would see her face, and she was complaining, in a voice pitched just above a whisper, about the price of eggs, which was the subject she chose whenever she was nervous, and she was nervous about everything. I was nervous about my shoes, which had been made for the woman I had been in October.

Rabbi Adler was not a man you heard about only in Southfield. He had been born in Hungary in 1911 and had come to Detroit in 1938 with his wife and a trunk of books that had taken him four months to get through the border bureaucracy. He had served in the Army during the war, had taught Talmud at Wayne State on Saturdays, and had a habit of walking home from services in the dark, in the deepest cold, because he said he had learned in Budapest that a man who cannot walk alone in the dark cannot stand anywhere else. He lectured at the Jewish Theological Seminary. He had a book published about the Talmud's treatment of hospitality, and the New York Times had reviewed it, which in those years was the closest thing a rabbi could get to a medal.

What he did every Shabbat morning, though, that no review ever covered, was tell the same story. It was about a knock at a door in 1943. He told it the way other men tell stories about their fathers or their wars, with the whole congregation rearranging itself to listen, men loosening their ties, women straightening their coats. "My family was in a small room in Budapest," he would begin, and he would say, "and there came a knock at the door, and my father looked up, and he said," and then he would pause, and let the pause sit in the room like something physical, and he never, in all the years I sat beneath him, told us what the father said. He would go on to something else: the blessings, the reading, the weather, the war in Southeast Asia, which was beginning to arrive in the papers with photographs that nobody wanted to look at for long.

He was mid-pause that morning when the shot went off.

I want to be exact about the sound, because people ask. It was not like a movie. It was a sharp, flat report, close, the way a car backfires when you are standing right beside it, and it had no echo to it at all, because the sanctuary was full of wool and bodies, which absorb sound. The first thing that happened after the report was not screaming. It was a silence with a texture to it, the candles at the ark still burning, the snow still falling outside the tall windows, and Rabbi Adler folding down into the front of the sanctuary like a man whose knees have been asked for something beyond them. He went down beside the ark, and he stayed down.

Then I saw him. The boy. He was standing in the aisle where he had been sitting, twenty-one years old, if I had known then what I know now, wearing a brown sport coat and a tie, and he was holding the gun with both hands, the way you hold something you are trying not to drop, and he was looking at the rabbi, or at where the rabbi was, and his face had the look of a man who has just done something he had decided to do and now wanted to see through.

Here is the part that has never come out right in any telling, and I will try once more. I moved toward him.

I was eight months pregnant and I moved toward him, and I want to be clear that I was not brave and I did not think about anything so large as courage. What I knew, in the fraction of a second between the first report and the second, was that he was young, and that I had seen him. That was the whole of it, the recognition. I had seen him at the youth rallies in the early sixties, standing in the back row with his hands in his pockets. I had seen him once, in January, helping Rabbi Adler carry a stack of books from the office to the front, and the rabbi had thanked him, and the two of them had stood there a moment longer than was necessary, the way men do when one of them is grateful and the other is trying not to show it.

I did not know his name yet. I did not know that in January he had come to the rabbi's office asking for a letter of recommendation, for a job at the parts warehouse on Ford Road, and that the rabbi had given him the letter and a handshake and, in my later reckoning, too little. I did not know that the papers, within the hour, would call him a stranger, a man with no ties to the congregation, which was a lie that protected everyone in that room, including me, because if he had been a stranger then the temple had known nothing, and the congregation had no reason to look at its own hands.

What I knew was that he was a boy I had seen carry books, and the rabbi was down, and I wanted to reach him. I want to say that plainly, because it is the sentence that has cost me fifty-three years of easy conversation. I wanted to reach him. I took a step, and then the temple decided otherwise.

A synagogue in February fills with bodies in a particular way, because the bodies are cold and heavy and want to get to the light. The men in the front turned, and the turning became a current, and the current reached the women's section and took hold of it, the way water takes hold of something lighter than itself. Mrs. Abramson grabbed my arm and pulled, and I grabbed at the air in the direction of the aisle, and neither of us was in control of anything. Elbow on my ribs. A stranger's coat brushing my face. Someone shouting the rabbi's name, then someone shouting a different name, then someone shouting nothing at all, just moving.

I was carried. That is the word I have always wanted to use, because it is true. I was carried out of the sanctuary and through the doors and into the snow, a package among packages, and my feet came along when the feet came along, and I could not separate myself from the flow any more than a leaf separates from a river. I tried to look back. I remember trying, with my whole body, to look back over the shoulder of the man in front of me, and I got one glimpse, not of the boy, of the doorway, the gray light of it, the shape of people still standing in it, and then the crowd had me at the steps, and the steps had the lot, and the lot had the street.

The second shot came then, or near then. It arrived through the roar of the crowd, muffled, closer than it should have been, and I understood its meaning before I understood anything else, which is to say that I understood, standing in the snow with my coat riding up over my stomach and Mrs. Abramson nowhere in sight, that I would never see the boy's face again. He had given me one look, and it had been the look of a man finishing something, and I had been denied the rest of it. The papers later said he had turned the gun on himself in the aisle, that he had died within minutes, that he had left no note and no family that anyone could find, and I believed every word of it and believed it the way you believe weather, without being able to say where the believing actually lives.

Bert came at ten o'clock. He had been working his Saturday shift at the Fisher Body plant, which is the reason he was not in the sanctuary, and I have spent some years thinking about whether he was relieved by that fact, and I have decided he was, slightly, and that he has never once let me see it, and that we have never once discussed it, and that this is how a marriage can hold a small unspoken stone for fifty years and never crack. He brought me coffee and a coat and drove me to the hospital, where I sat in a waiting room that smelled of soap and listened to a nurse ask me, gently, what had happened, and I told her about a car accident on Grand River, because it was February and there were always car accidents on Grand River, and because the truth had no shape that a nurse could hold.

Mrs. Abramson was in the hospital too, on a different floor, with a bruised hip from the steps. She told her story, when I finally found her, and her story was different. In her version she had run for the door immediately, and had been sensible, and had been swept along by other people's fear, which she described as a kind of weather. She did not say she had tried to reach the boy. I asked her, and she looked at me for a long moment with an expression I have never forgotten, which was not hostility but something more careful, the look of a woman deciding how much of her own interior she could afford to show another woman on a hospital bed. She said she had not been in the room long enough to know what had happened. I believed her the way you believe weather.

The papers' theories arrived that Sunday. A stranger, they said. A stranger with mental illness, a stranger with a grudge over money, a stranger whose name, once they found it, was Leonard Blum, and who had worked at a warehouse on Ford Road and had asked a rabbi for a letter of recommendation in January and had received one. I read the papers and I did not correct anyone, because correcting anyone would have required admitting that I had known him, which would have required admitting that I had seen him in the back row and had not spoken to him, and that the temple had let him drift for two years without asking him one question, and that I was in that temple every Saturday and had asked nothing either.

The rabbi's relatives came from New York and from the Bronx, and they were dignified and exhausted, and one of them, a cousin, a man named Saul who taught history, told me, in the weeks afterward, that Rabbi Adler had finished the story once, for an audience I was not part of. The knock at the door in 1943, Saul said, had been the father. The father had come in and said that dinner was ready. That was the whole of it. A knock, and dinner. The great suspense of Rabbi Adler's life ended with a meal being served, and I sat with that for a long time, and I am not sure whether it comforted me or whether it offended me, because I wanted the rabbi's story to be about something larger than the moment he was interrupted. The interruption, it turned out, had been larger.

The baby came in May, three weeks early, in the hospital in Troy, and he was a boy, and we named him Aaron after the rabbi, which Bert said at the time was only right, and which I have sometimes thought of as an obligation we took on without reading the terms. Aaron is fifty-three now. He lives in Rochester with a wife named Doreen and a daughter in college, and he has no memory of February 12th, 1966, and none of the things he does not remember are any lighter for having been carried by me instead.

The temple still stands. This is not what most people expect when I tell them the story, because they have learned to expect the parking lot, the memorial plaque, the restaurant with the menu board. But Temple Beth Sholom is still there on its street in Southfield, with its snow-buried lot and its windows that light up on Saturday mornings, and I have driven past it every February for fifty-three years, and it has never once seemed to me like a monument. It is just a building where people go to stand in wool coats and wait for someone to finish a sentence.

This year, on the anniversary, I drove past it and I turned off the radio and I sat in the lot for a while, which was more than I had done in decades. The sky was the color of February always is, the particular gray that has given up on becoming anything else. Inside, I could see the shapes of people through the tall windows, standing, leaning, talking.

I did not go in. And I did not, that night, tell Aaron the whole of it, the part about my moving toward the boy, the part about being carried away like a parcel, the part about the two seconds that belonged to me and were taken by the crowd's arithmetic, which is that ninety bodies in a cold room in February will always outweigh one. He asked me how I felt about the anniversary, and I told him the true but smaller version, which is that I had driven past the temple and thought about Rabbi Adler's knock at the door and the dinner that was waiting behind it. He said that was strange, and I said it was strange, and we had our meal.

The two seconds are still mine. I have never given them back to anyone, and I am not sure I could find the place where the crowd took them to return them. There is a boy who died in a brown sport coat on a Saturday morning in Southfield, and I know his name now, and I have never said it aloud, and if I am honest, which I am not usually, I have never wanted to say it aloud either, because saying it would make it a person I had failed to reach, and I have had fifty-three years to live with that and I have made it fit.

What I cannot make fit is the sentence itself. My father looked up, and he said. I have waited half a century for that sentence to be finished, and it was finished once, by a cousin in a hospital hallway, with dinner as its content, and it is still unfinished to me, because the rabbi never said it himself, and I was in the room when he stopped, and I am the only one who knows that the pause was not a pause at all. It was the rest of his life, cut off mid-word, and the snow falling on the windows, and a young man standing in an aisle holding a gun with both hands, and a woman in bad shoes who wanted, for two seconds, to reach him.
